# Environment and benchmarks {#sec-environment}

This section defines the two data-generating families, the benchmark forecasters and the diagnostics. Everything in it is computed by the simulator, benchmark and diagnostic code of the repository (`rt/sim.py`, `rt/bayes.py`, `rt/diagnostics.py`), whose contents are bound to the pre-registration by a hash ([Appendix @sec-app-prereg]).

## Two families of series

**Family A** carries every hypothesis. A sequence is generated by

$$
x_0 = 0, \qquad x_t = \rho\, x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, 1), \qquad \rho \sim U[0, 1],
$$ {#eq-family-a}

with ρ drawn once per sequence. The mean (zero) and the noise scale (one) are known to every forecaster, and $x_0$ is never an input. The only unknown is ρ, so that learning ρ is the whole of the forecasting problem.

**Family B** is used only for the descriptive overlay of @sec-overlay and the illustrative comparison of @sec-spf; no hypothesis reads it. It is the same process around an unknown mean μ with an unknown scale σ:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &\sim \mathrm{InvGamma}(a, b), \qquad \mu \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(0,\, k\sigma^2), \\
x_0 &= \mu, \qquad x_t = \mu + \rho\,(x_{t-1} - \mu) + \sigma\,\varepsilon_t,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-family-b}

with shape $a$ = {{< var design.b.a >}}, scale $b$ = {{< var design.b.b >}} (so that σ² has prior mean one) and $k$ = {{< var design.b.k >}}, and again ρ ~ U[0, 1]. An experimental subject is not told the mean or the scale of the series, so Family B is the closer analogue of the laboratory task.

Each path is simulated to t = {{< var design.t_sim >}}, so that a target exists at every horizon $h$ = 1, …, {{< var design.horizons >}} for every forecast origin $t$ = 1, …, {{< var design.t_max >}}. Write $F_{t,h}$ for a forecast of $x_{t+h}$ made at origin $t$.

## The full-information forecast

A forecaster who knows ρ (and, in Family B, μ) forecasts

$$
F^{\mathrm{FI}}_{t,h} = \rho^{h} x_t \quad\text{(Family A)}, \qquad F^{\mathrm{FI}}_{t,h} = \mu + \rho^{h}(x_t - \mu) \quad\text{(Family B)}.
$$ {#eq-fire}

This is the full-information rational forecast against which the experimental and survey literatures measure over- and underreaction. It is reported descriptively and is not used by any hypothesis, as is a least-squares learner (a regression of $x_s$ on $x_{s-1}$ with an intercept over the observations so far, iterated $h$ steps), reported as the familiar frequentist learner.

## Bayes with the full window

A forecaster who knows the family but not ρ holds the training prior, ρ ~ U[0, 1], and updates it on $x_{1:t} = (x_1, \dots, x_t)$. In Family A the first observation is $x_1 = \varepsilon_1$, whose distribution does not depend on ρ, so the likelihood is the product of the transition densities and the log-likelihood is, up to a term free of ρ,

$$
\ell_t(\rho) = \rho\, S_{xy} - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho^{2} S_{xx}, \qquad
S_{xy} = \sum_{j=2}^{t} x_j x_{j-1}, \qquad S_{xx} = \sum_{j=2}^{t} x_{j-1}^{2}.
$$ {#eq-loglik-full}

The posterior density on [0, 1] is proportional to $\exp \ell_t(\rho)$, a normal density in ρ truncated to the unit interval. Because future shocks are independent of the past, $E[x_{t+h} \mid \rho, x_{1:t}] = \rho^{h} x_t$, and the Bayes forecast is

$$
F^{\mathrm{B}}_{t,h} = E\!\left[\rho^{h} \mid x_{1:t}\right] x_t .
$$ {#eq-bayes}

The posterior moments are computed on a grid of $G$ = {{< var design.grid_points >}} equally spaced points $\rho_g$ on [0, 1] by the trapezoid rule,

$$
E\!\left[\rho^{h} \mid x_{1:t}\right] \approx \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{G} w_g\, \rho_g^{h}\, e^{\ell_t(\rho_g)}}{\sum_{g=1}^{G} w_g\, e^{\ell_t(\rho_g)}},
\qquad w_1 = w_G = \tfrac{1}{2},\quad w_g = 1 \text{ otherwise},
$$ {#eq-grid}

with the same weights in numerator and denominator and the exponentials normalised in log space. We call this benchmark *Bayes*. It is exact up to the quadrature, which the tests of the repository check against a brute-force computation.

## Window-Bayes: the same forecaster with the network's information

A network with memory length $W$ sees, at origin $t$, only the last W observations and their time indices. Its information set is

$$
\mathcal{I}^{W}_{t} = \left(x_s, x_{s+1}, \dots, x_t;\; t\right), \qquad s = \max(1,\; t - W + 1).
$$ {#eq-info}

The benchmark for such a network is the Bayes forecaster with the same prior and the same information set. Deriving it requires one step beyond @eq-loglik-full: the first observation in the window is no longer uninformative. Iterating @eq-family-a from $x_0 = 0$,

$$
x_s = \sum_{k=0}^{s-1} \rho^{k}\, \varepsilon_{s-k}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_s \mid \rho \sim N\!\left(0,\; V_s(\rho)\right), \qquad V_s(\rho) = \sum_{k=0}^{s-1} \rho^{2k}.
$$ {#eq-first-obs}

$V_s(\rho)$ is the variance the process has accumulated by time $s$. It equals one for every ρ when $s = 1$, equals $s$ at ρ = 1, and rises towards the stationary variance $1/(1-\rho^{2})$ as $s$ grows for ρ below one. The size of $x_s$ relative to the unit shocks is therefore evidence about ρ, and how much evidence depends on $s$, which is why the time index belongs to the information set. The density of the window given ρ is $p(x_s \mid \rho)\prod_{j=s+1}^{t} \varphi(x_j - \rho x_{j-1})$, with φ the standard normal density, so the log-likelihood is, up to a term free of ρ,

$$
\ell^{W}_{t}(\rho) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log V_s(\rho) \;-\; \frac{x_s^{2}}{2\,V_s(\rho)} \;+\; \rho\, S_{xy} \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\rho^{2} S_{xx},
$$ {#eq-loglik-window}

where $S_{xy} = \sum_{j=s+1}^{t} x_j x_{j-1}$ and $S_{xx} = \sum_{j=s+1}^{t} x_{j-1}^{2}$ now run over the transitions inside the window.

The *window-Bayes* forecast is

$$
F^{\mathrm{WB}}_{t,h} = E\!\left[\rho^{h} \mid \mathcal{I}^{W}_{t}\right] x_t ,
$$ {#eq-window-bayes}

with the posterior moment computed on the same grid as @eq-grid with $\ell^{W}_{t}$ in place of $\ell_t$. In the code $V_s$ is computed as the direct sum of @eq-first-obs, not from the closed form $(1-\rho^{2s})/(1-\rho^{2})$, so that it is exact at ρ = 1 and free of cancellation near it. For the full window $s = 1$, the first two terms of @eq-loglik-window are free of ρ, and window-Bayes is Bayes.

In Family B the same construction applies with μ and σ² integrated analytically. Given ρ, the window is a Gaussian linear regression in μ with $m = t - s + 1$ rows $y_i = z_i \mu + \sigma e_i$: the first observation contributes $y = x_s/\sqrt{V_s}$ and $z = 1/\sqrt{V_s}$, since $x_s \mid \rho, \mu, \sigma \sim N(\mu, \sigma^{2}V_s)$, and each transition $j = s+1, \dots, t$ contributes $y = x_j - \rho x_{j-1}$ and $z = 1 - \rho$. Under the Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior of @eq-family-b,

$$
L = \frac{1}{k} + \frac{1}{V_s} + (t-s)(1-\rho)^{2}, \qquad
S_{zy} = \frac{x_s}{V_s} + (1-\rho)\sum_{j=s+1}^{t}(x_j - \rho x_{j-1}), \qquad
Q = \sum_i y_i^{2} - \frac{S_{zy}^{2}}{L},
$$

$$
E[\mu \mid \rho, \mathcal{I}] = \frac{S_{zy}}{L}, \qquad
\log p(\mathcal{I} \mid \rho) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log V_s - \tfrac{1}{2}\log L - \left(a + \tfrac{m}{2}\right)\log\!\left(b + \tfrac{Q}{2}\right) + \text{const},
$$ {#eq-family-b-post}

and the forecast is the posterior mean over ρ, on the same grid, of $\rho^{h} x_t + (1-\rho^{h})\,S_{zy}/L$.

## Window-Bayes is the squared-error optimum

::: {#prp-optimal}
## Window-Bayes minimises expected squared error

Let $(\rho, x_1, x_2, \dots)$ be drawn from Family A with ρ ~ U[0, 1]. Fix an origin $t$, a window $W$ and a horizon $h$, and let $\mathcal{I} = \mathcal{I}^{W}_{t}$. Among all measurable functions $f$ of $\mathcal{I}$ with $E[f(\mathcal{I})^{2}] < \infty$, the expected squared error $E[(x_{t+h} - f(\mathcal{I}))^{2}]$ is minimised, uniquely up to null sets, by the window-Bayes forecast $f^{*}(\mathcal{I}) = E[\rho^{h} \mid \mathcal{I}]\, x_t$. Consequently the training loss of a network with window W, squared error summed over horizons and averaged over origins and sequences drawn from the prior, is minimised over all functions of the network's inputs by the window-Bayes forecast at every origin and horizon.
:::

::: {.proof}
All second moments are finite, since $E[x_t^{2}] \le t$. For any admissible $f$ write $x_{t+h} - f = (x_{t+h} - m) + (m - f)$ with $m = E[x_{t+h} \mid \mathcal{I}]$. The cross term has expectation zero, because $m - f$ is a function of $\mathcal{I}$ and $E[x_{t+h} - m \mid \mathcal{I}] = 0$, so

$$
E\!\left[(x_{t+h} - f)^{2}\right] = E\!\left[(x_{t+h} - m)^{2}\right] + E\!\left[(m - f)^{2}\right] \;\ge\; E\!\left[(x_{t+h} - m)^{2}\right],
$$

with equality only if $f = m$ almost surely. It remains to show that $m$ is the window-Bayes forecast. Iterating @eq-family-a forward, $x_{t+h} = \rho^{h} x_t + \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \rho^{k} \varepsilon_{t+h-k}$, and the shocks after t are independent of $(\rho, x_{1:t})$ with mean zero, so $E[x_{t+h} \mid \rho, x_{1:t}] = \rho^{h} x_t$. The pair $(\rho, \mathcal{I})$ is a function of $(\rho, x_{1:t})$ and $\rho^{h} x_t$ is a function of $(\rho, \mathcal{I})$, so by the tower property $E[x_{t+h} \mid \rho, \mathcal{I}] = \rho^{h} x_t$ and $m = E[\rho^{h} x_t \mid \mathcal{I}] = E[\rho^{h} \mid \mathcal{I}]\, x_t$, since $x_t$ belongs to $\mathcal{I}$. By Bayes' rule the conditional density of ρ given $\mathcal{I}$ is proportional on [0, 1] to the prior density, which is constant, times the density of the window given ρ, which is $\exp \ell^{W}_{t}(\rho)$ up to a factor free of ρ by @eq-first-obs and @eq-loglik-window. Hence $m$ is @eq-window-bayes.

For the training loss, a network with window W computes at each origin a function $f_{t,h}$ of the inputs $\mathcal{I}^{W}_{t}$, the time index among them, and the loss is $E_t \sum_{h} E[(x_{t+h} - f_{t,h}(\mathcal{I}^{W}_{t}))^{2}]$, with the outer expectation over the distribution of origins used in training. This is a non-negatively weighted sum of the terms just treated, with a separate function for each $(t, h)$, so it is minimised by minimising each term.
:::

Three remarks fix what the proposition does and does not say. First, the optimum is an optimum on average over the prior. At a single fixed ρ a forecaster that leans towards that ρ has lower squared error than window-Bayes there, and must then have higher error elsewhere under the prior. That is why the excess-error margin is two-sided (@sec-prereg): a network that beats its benchmark at a fixed ρ by more than the margin is not "equivalent" to it. Second, the proposition makes H1 and H2 tests of approximation and optimisation, not of rationality. The minimum is over all functions of the inputs. A network attains it only if its function class contains window-Bayes, or comes arbitrarily close, and training finds that member. A finite network trained for a finite number of steps can fall short on either count, and the design does not separate the two. Whether it reaches the optimum, and in which direction it misses, is an empirical matter. Third, the proposition is silent on H3's direction: any miss could be an overreaction or an underreaction relative to the benchmark, and nothing in the argument says which. The same argument holds in Family B with (μ, σ², ρ) in place of ρ, since the prior of @eq-family-b gives σ² a finite mean and hence every $x_t$ a finite second moment.

## What a Bayesian looks like from outside

@fig-benchmarks and @tbl-benchmarks show the benchmarks alone, with no network involved. Full Bayes has implied persistence {{< var bench.bayes.r00 >}} at ρ = 0 and {{< var bench.bayes.r10 >}} at ρ = 1: it is pulled towards the interior of the prior at both ends, and by this measure overreacts against the truth at low ρ. Window-Bayes is pulled further, to {{< var bench.w4.r00 >}} at ρ = 0 with four observations and {{< var bench.w2.r00 >}} with two. At ρ = 0.8 its implied persistence is {{< var bench.w4.r08 >}} with four observations and {{< var bench.w16.r08 >}} with sixteen, below the truth: at ρ = {{< var design.h3.rho_lo >}} and {{< var design.h3.rho_hi >}}, window-Bayes underreacts against the truth at every one of the four finite windows. Across the grid, window-Bayes differs from full Bayes by up to {{< var bench.max_wb_minus_bayes >}} in implied persistence. For scale, people's implied persistence in the experiment of @afrouzi2023overreaction exceeds ρ by {{< var human.excess_min >}} to {{< var human.excess_max >}} for ρ up to 0.8. A network judged against the truth, or against full Bayes, would thus appear biased by an amount of the same order as the human effect merely for having a short window. Averaged over the prior, by contrast, these forecasters have almost the same implied persistence ({{< var bench.bayes.prior >}} for Bayes and {{< var bench.w4.prior >}} for window-Bayes with four observations, against {{< var bench.fire.prior >}} for full information), which is the sense in which each is unbiased.

## Diagnostics

All diagnostics pool (sequence, origin) pairs over the forecast origins $t$ = {{< var design.eval_t_first >}}, …, {{< var design.eval_t_last >}}, the rounds on which @afrouzi2023overreaction score their subjects, and drop pairs with a missing value. Let slope($y$ on $z$) denote the ordinary least-squares slope of $y$ on $z$ with an intercept over those pairs. For a forecaster F, a benchmark $B$ and a horizon $h$:

- **Implied persistence** is $\mathrm{IP}_h(F) = \mathrm{slope}(F_{t,h} \text{ on } x_t)$. For the full-information forecast it is $\rho^{h}$.
- The **gap** is $\mathrm{IP}_h(\text{model}) - \mathrm{IP}_h(B)$. A positive gap means that the model reacts more to the current value than the benchmark with the same information: overreaction beyond it. A negative gap is underreaction beyond it.
- **Excess error** is a ratio of means, in percentage points of the benchmark's mean squared error:

    $$
    100\left(\frac{\operatorname{mean}\bigl[(x_{t+h} - F^{\text{model}}_{t,h})^{2}\bigr]}{\operatorname{mean}\bigl[(x_{t+h} - F^{B}_{t,h})^{2}\bigr]} - 1\right),
    $$

    with both means taken over the same pooled pairs, those where both forecasts exist.
- The **error-on-revision coefficient** is $b_h = \mathrm{slope}\bigl(x_{t+h} - F_{t,h} \text{ on } F_{t,h} - F_{t-1,h+1}\bigr)$ for $h = 1, \dots, 5$, the individual-level regression of @bordalo2020overreaction. A positive b means that errors follow revisions (underreaction); a negative b means overreaction. A revision at horizon $h$ needs the forecast at horizon $h + 1$ from the period before, which is why the networks forecast {{< var design.horizons >}} horizons.
- **κ** is $\mathrm{slope}\bigl(F^{\text{model}}_{t,1} - F^{\mathrm{B}}_{t,1} \text{ on } x_t - F^{\mathrm{B}}_{t-1,1}\bigr)$, the response of the model's one-step deviation from full Bayes to the Bayes surprise.

The confirmatory hypotheses read the gap and the excess error at horizon 1; the error-on-revision coefficient, κ and the longer horizons are exploratory (@sec-exploratory). Two properties of the error-on-revision coefficient should be kept in mind. For full Bayes on data drawn from the prior it is zero, because the revision is known at $t$ and the error is unpredictable from anything known at $t$; the repository's gate, a set of checks that must pass before any run starts (@sec-prereg), confirms this, finding {{< var eor.gate.a >}} in Family A and {{< var eor.gate.b >}} in Family B. For window-Bayes it is not zero, even on prior-drawn data, because the forecast at $t - 1$ was made from a window that contains an observation the window at $t$ has dropped, so the two information sets are not nested and the revision is not known to the forecaster at $t$. And at a fixed ρ it is not zero for any learner. The coefficient is therefore compared with the benchmark's own, never with zero.

Family B sequences differ in level and scale, so a regression pooled over raw values would mostly measure differences between sequences in the mean, not how a forecast responds to news within a sequence. Every Family B diagnostic is therefore computed on standardised deviations $(x - \mu)/\sigma$ and $(F - \mu)/\sigma$, using each sequence's true μ and σ, identically for the model and every benchmark. Family A is used raw.
